grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: To jest koperta. Jan widzi kopertę. To jest pudełko. Jan otwiera pudełko.
grammar.note_en:
A noun’s case shows its job in a Polish sentence. The nominative is the naming form and the form used for a subject, the person or thing the sentence is about. The accusative is the usual form for the direct object of the affirmative action verbs taught here: it names what someone sees, takes, puts, opens or reads. To jest koperta means “This is an envelope”; Jan widzi kopertę means “Jan sees an envelope”. The noun is the same word, but its ending changes because its job changes. The subject Jan has not changed. Kopertę is not a different kind of envelope.

For these singular feminine nouns, replace the final -a with -ę: koperta → kopertę (“envelope”), lampa → lampę (“lamp”), litera → literę (“letter of the alphabet”), taśma → taśmę (“tape”), linia → linię (“line”), strzałka → strzałkę (“arrow”). In linia, keep the i in the stem: lini- plus ę gives linię. Change only the final a; the i remains part of the stem. The first table gives naming forms beside object forms already used in the story. It is a reference, not a table to fill in.

The neuter nouns here have the same nominative and accusative spelling: pudełko (“box”), narzędzie (“tool”), koło (“circle”), dno (“bottom”). To jest pudełko means “This is a box”; Jan otwiera pudełko means “Jan opens the box”. To jest dno means “This is the bottom”; Jan widzi dno means “Jan sees the bottom”. An unchanged ending does not mean that the noun has no case: its role is different even when the spelling is the same. Masculine inanimate nouns such as klucz (“key”), papier (“paper”), napis (“inscription”) and sznurek (“string”) also keep their spelling in these affirmative object examples. This is not a rule for every masculine noun or for people.

The action forms remain third-person singular: they describe one named person. Bierze means “takes/is taking”; kładzie means “puts/places”; otwiera means “opens/is opening”; widzi means “sees”; czyta means “reads/is reading”. Jan bierze klucz means “Jan takes the key”; Ala kładzie kopertę tu means “Ala puts the envelope here”; Ala otwiera kopertę means “Ala opens the envelope”; Jan czyta napis means “Jan reads the inscription”. The diagrams distinguish taking an object into a hand from putting it down, and beginning to lift a lid from seeing the contents after the lid is raised. Polish uses these single present-tense forms where English may use “is taking” or “is opening”. Potem means “then/afterwards”, connecting successive actions. It does not create a special verb tense.

Looking and seeing are related but distinct: Jan patrzy means “Jan looks”; Jan widzi kopertę means “Jan sees an envelope”. The newly opened box makes the envelope visible. Czy begins the bounded yes/no questions already met: Czy to jest narzędzie? means “Is this a tool?” Nie. To jest koperta means “No. This is an envelope”. This rejects an identification; it is not a negated action such as “does not have an envelope”. Negated direct objects and expressions meaning that something is absent come next chapter. Do not form an untaught negative object by putting nie before every verb here.

The large lock on the old sheet belongs to a przykład, an example or practice model. It is not the physical lock opened with the small key. Napis means written wording or an inscription; litera is one alphabet letter within that wording. The tape initially hides part of the recipient name. After it is removed, Jan reads Ala, and Ala opens that envelope. The string and tape are put aside; the box stays open after its lid is fully raised. On the newly removed sheet, lampa names a drawn lamp. Seeing that drawing does not establish where the physical lamp is. The ending asks that question without yet using the absence construction taught in chapter 3.

Table translations: To jest koperta / Jan widzi kopertę means “This is an envelope / Jan sees an envelope”; To jest lampa / Ala widzi lampę means “This is a lamp / Ala sees a lamp”; To jest litera / Jan czyta literę means “This is a letter / Jan reads the letter”; To jest taśma / Ala bierze taśmę means “This is tape / Ala takes the tape”; To jest linia / Ala widzi linię means “This is a line / Ala sees a line”; To jest strzałka / Jan widzi strzałkę means “This is an arrow / Jan sees an arrow”. The unchanged-form table reads To jest pudełko / Jan otwiera pudełko (“This is a box / Jan opens the box”), To jest dno / Jan widzi dno (“This is the bottom / Jan sees the bottom”), and To jest koło / Ala widzi koło (“This is a circle / Ala sees a circle”).

obrazec.rule: Wyrazy: koperta, lampa, narzędzie, litera, klucz, rysunek, stół, znak. 1: envelope; 2: lamp; 3: tool; 4: letter (A).
Wyrazy: sznurek, taśma, strzałka, napis, koło, linia, dno, przykład. 5: string; 6: tape; 7: arrow; 8: inscription.

items.rubric: Name the actual small lock, the physical box, or both: Jan opens each in this section. Jan otwiera zamek and Jan otwiera pudełko are both correct. Do not claim he opens the large drawn practice lock. Other true Polish word orders are valid.

Accept any object Jan actually sees in the Pudełko section: the envelope, bottom, tape, letter, inscription, string, or another object visibly present there. A truthful stage-specific answer is valid; no physical lamp or repair tool is found inside the box. The model gives two of several correct possibilities.

Accept any reading in the Koperta section: the recipient wording Ala, the worked practice example, or the lamp caption Lampa. Each is explicitly read there. A sentence identifying what Jan reads is valid; the question does not silently restrict you to one moment.
Ala opens the envelope bearing her name and removes the illustrated sheet. Keep Ala as the actor asked about; other true word orders are valid.

Refer to the new sheet labelled Lampa, which has a line ending in an arrow, Ala’s added circle and a depicted lamp. Name at least one of those features in a truthful Polish sentence, using the accusative object form where it changes. The old practice sheet’s box drawing is a different sheet in the comparison.
Jan reads the lamp caption on the new sheet, not the old practice sheet or envelope name. The question does not ask you to invent the missing physical lamp’s location.
